facts.statement: The first fossils of Toyotamaphimeia were found on May 3, 1964, while building a new school at Osaka University.
facts.quote: The first bones belonging to Toyotamaphimeia were discovered on May 3, 1964, during the construction of a new school building on the grounds of Ôsaka University.

facts.statement: Toyotamaphimeia was a large crocodylian that measured between 6.3 and 7.3 meters in length.
facts.quote: Toyotamaphimeia was a fairly large crocodylian measuring approximately 6.3 - 7.3 m long.

facts.statement: The skull of Toyotamaphimeia was triangular and longirostrine.
facts.quote: Toyotamaphimeia's skull is triangular in shape and longirostrine.

facts.statement: The skull of Toyotamaphimeia measured over 1 meter from the tip of the premaxilla to the back of the parietal bone.
facts.quote: It's fairly large, measuring over 1 m from the tip of the premaxillary to the posterior end of the parietal.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence shows healed fractures in the tibia, fibula, and mandible, as well as healing bite marks on osteoderms.
facts.quote: The mandible is broken off at the tip, the tibia and fibula have been fractured and healed and some of the osteoderms present preserve healing bite marks.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the healed injuries on the holotype specimen may have resulted from intraspecific fights and possibly indicate it was a male.
facts.quote: Katsura suggests that they may have been the result of intraspecific fights, furthermore hypothesizing that this could mean the Osaka University specimen may have been a male.

facts.statement: Toyotamaphimeia lived in Japan and Taiwan during the Middle Pleistocene.
facts.quote: Toyotamaphimeia (named after Toyotama-hime) is a genus of extinct gavialid crocodylian which lived in Japan and Taiwan during the Middle Pleistocene.

facts.statement: Toyotamaphimeia lived at the northern thermal limit for crocodilians in Japan.
facts.quote: At this latitude Toyotamaphimeia would have existed at the thermal limit of crocodilians.

facts.statement: Morphological studies classify Toyotamaphimeia as a basal member of Gavialinae, related to Penghusuchus and Hanyusuchus.
facts.quote: Following this interpretation, Iijima et al. found Toyotamaphimeia to have been a basal member of Gavialinae, clading together with the Miocene Penghusuchus and the then newly named Hanyusuchus.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Toyotamaphimeia originated in Japan or Taiwan, with some researchers arguing it evolved in Taiwan and migrated north.
facts.quote: Cho and Tsai argued that Toyotamaphimeia originated in Taiwan and evolved to acquire a large body size with gigantothermic physiology, and that it eventually migrated out of Taiwan and dispersed farther north to Japan.

facts.statement: Toyotamaphimeia is classified within the family Gavialidae, though its exact placement is sometimes noted as uncertain.
The fossil record for Toyotamaphimeia spans from the Piacenzian to the Chibanian, between 3.6 and 0.129 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Piacenzian to Chibanian (3.6 to 0.129 million years ago)

rejected.statement: The genus Toyotamaphimeia was established in 1983, 18 years after the initial discovery, when researchers realized the skull was distinct from Tomistoma.
rejected.quote: In 1983, 18 years after the initial discovery, the skull was redescribed and deemed different enough from Tomistoma to erect a new genus, Toyotamaphimeia creating the comb. nov. Toyotamaphimeia machikanensis.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'in 1983 18 years after the initial discovery'
